script.opening: (Wife, husband present and somewhat indifferent.) "I don’t recognise my husband any more. Over the last year or two Brian’s become rude and tactless — says awful things in public — he’s spent thousands on nonsense, he doesn’t seem to care about anything or anyone, and he’s eating strangely. His memory’s actually fine. People say it’s a midlife crisis or stress, but this isn’t him. He doesn’t think anything’s wrong."

facts.text: Wife, Carol (56), and Brian (58), sitting together. Brian agrees to Carol speaking: "If she wants. I’m fine."

Over about 2 years: makes rude comments about people’s weight in shops, told a neighbour her husband’s funeral was "a waste of a Saturday", no embarrassment afterwards. Lost interest in his grandchildren and hobbies. Doesn’t react when Carol is upset — "as if he’s switched off".
Spent about £12,000 on online gadgets and a second car they don’t need; signed up to several subscriptions. Carol found out from the bank statements. He still has full access to their accounts.
Craves sweets — eats a whole packet of biscuits at once; put on a stone. Insists on the same meal every day. Repeats the same phrases and walks the same route at the same time daily.

Memory for events and appointments is fine; doesn’t get lost. No hallucinations. Not low or tearful; no talk of suicide. No headaches, no fits, no weakness, no swallowing problems, no twitching. Drinks 2 pints a week. No head injury.

Was a bank branch manager; took early retirement last year after complaints about his "attitude". Still drives daily; Carol thinks he drives faster and closer to other cars and "doesn’t seem to notice".
Carol doesn’t know of anything in the family — Brian’s parents died young (accident and heart attack). No regular medicines; no allergies.

Carol: tearful, exhausted, relieved to be taken seriously; becomes upset if it is brushed off as stress. Brian: flat, unconcerned, a little inappropriate ("Can we hurry up?"), denies any problem. If the word dementia is used, Carol says: "Dementia? But his memory’s fine."

ice.ideas: Carol: "Everyone keeps saying stress. I think something is actually wrong with him." Brian: "Nothing’s wrong with me."
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — Carol is frightened about money (the spending is draining their savings), about his driving, and that their marriage is over and she is scared of what it might be.
ice.expectations: Carol: "For someone to find out what this is, and help me know what to do about the money."

cues: "His memory’s actually fine" — a dementia that does not start with memory.
"He’s spent thousands" — financial risk and lasting power of attorney.
"He still drives every day" (if asked) — driving safety and DVLA.

checkpoints.text: Recognises FRONTOTEMPORAL DEMENTIA (behavioural variant; Pick’s is a pathological subtype) — early personality/behaviour change (disinhibition, loss of empathy, apathy, impulsivity/reckless spending, altered eating) with relatively preserved memory and poor insight, young-onset
Does NOT mislabel it as a midlife crisis/stress/primary psychiatric illness — recognising personality change in a younger adult warrants considering an organic/neurodegenerative cause

Takes a COLLATERAL history with Brian’s consent (spouse essential given poor insight) and screens the differential (depression, bipolar/mania, psychosis, alcohol/substance, other dementias, MND overlap, family history, structural/endocrine — NICE NG97 bloods + cognitive assessment, not excluding dementia on a normal score)

Assesses RISK/safeguarding — financial vulnerability/reckless spending (lasting power of attorney discussed now while he may have capacity), behavioural risk, and DRIVING (DVLA duty; no driving pending assessment if judgement is a concern)

REFERS to a specialist dementia diagnostic/young-onset/neurology service for assessment (cognitive testing, neuroimaging), knowing NG97 advises against acetylcholinesterase inhibitors or memantine in FTD
SUPPORTS the carer — validates the distress, explains it is an illness not a choice (so the patient isn’t blamed), and signposts carer support, including a carer’s assessment (Care Act 2014)
Communicates sensitively with both the patient (poor insight) and the spouse, and checks understanding
Safety-nets and follows up: referral to a young-onset dementia service, basic investigations, risk/finance/driving advice, carer support, and review — recognising FTD, not dismissing it as stress

worked.txt: "Thank you for describing it so clearly — and you know him best. A real change in personality like this, over a year or two in someone Brian’s age, is NOT just a midlife crisis or stress; it can be a medical condition affecting the front of the brain, and it deserves proper assessment."

"One cause of exactly this pattern — becoming disinhibited, less empathetic, impulsive with money, with memory actually preserved — is a type of dementia called frontotemporal dementia. It often gets missed because the memory is fine and people assume it’s behaviour or stress."

"Brian, is it all right with you if your wife tells me what she’s noticed? Your account is invaluable, because Brian may not feel anything’s wrong. I’d like to examine Brian in person, and I’ll do some blood tests — blood count, calcium, sugar, kidney, liver and thyroid tests, B12 and folate — and a cognitive check, and think about other causes like depression or alcohol, to be thorough. A normal memory test wouldn’t rule this out. Has anyone in the family had dementia, motor neurone disease or mental illness?"

"A couple of practical things: the spending may need protecting, and it’s worth thinking about a lasting power of attorney now, while Brian can make that decision himself. And I have to ask about driving — I’d advise not driving while this is assessed, and if dementia is diagnosed it must be declared to the DVLA. I know that’s hard."

"I’m referring Brian to a young-onset dementia/neurology service for detailed assessment and a scan. And importantly — how are YOU coping? This is bewildering, and none of it is his fault or yours. There’s support for carers, including a carer’s assessment from the council, and I’ll connect you."
"Come back if things escalate or there’s any risk to him or others. We’ll get the assessment moving and support you both through it."

f.learning: FRONTOTEMPORAL DEMENTIA (FTD), here the behavioural variant (bvFTD; Pick’s disease is a pathological subtype, not a synonym), is a YOUNG-ONSET dementia (often 50s–60s) presenting with early PERSONALITY and BEHAVIOUR change — disinhibition (socially inappropriate remarks/actions), loss of EMPATHY, apathy, impulsivity and poor judgement (e.g. reckless spending), repetitive/compulsive behaviours and altered eating — with relatively PRESERVED memory early on and often POOR INSIGHT (a language variant presents with progressive speech/language decline). It is frequently MISATTRIBUTED to a midlife crisis, stress, relationship breakdown, depression or primary psychiatric illness, causing diagnostic delay, so personality change of this kind in a younger adult — especially with a clear timeline and collateral history — should prompt consideration of an organic/neurodegenerative cause rather than "just stress". Take a COLLATERAL history with the patient’s consent (the spouse is essential given poor insight) and screen the differential (depression, bipolar/mania, psychosis, alcohol/substance misuse, other dementias such as Alzheimer’s which is memory-led, FTD–motor neurone disease overlap, family history, and structural/endocrine/metabolic causes — examination face to face, NICE NG97 bloods (FBC, calcium, glucose, renal and liver function, thyroid function, B12 and folate) and a cognitive assessment, remembering NG97 advises not ruling out dementia on a normal cognitive score alone). Assess RISK and safeguarding: financial vulnerability/reckless spending (lasting power of attorney discussed now, while he may have capacity — Mental Capacity Act 2005), behavioural risk, and DRIVING (a person diagnosed with dementia must notify the DVLA; advise not driving while assessed if judgement is a concern). Refer to a specialist dementia diagnostic service — a YOUNG-ONSET DEMENTIA service/cognitive neurology clinic at this age — for detailed cognitive testing and neuroimaging (NG97 advises against acetylcholinesterase inhibitors or memantine in FTD), and crucially SUPPORT THE CARER — validating the distress, explaining it is an illness not a choice (so the patient is not blamed), offering a carer’s assessment (Care Act 2014; NICE NG150) and signposting carer support. The skill is recognising young-onset behavioural-variant dementia, taking a collateral history, excluding mimics, addressing risk/driving, referring, and supporting the family — not mislabelling it stress.

knowledge.guideline: [1] NICE NG97 Dementia: assessment, management and support for people living with dementia and their carers (2018) · [2] International consensus criteria for behavioural-variant frontotemporal dementia, Rascovsky et al., Brain 2011 (international) · [3] DVLA Assessing fitness to drive: dementia · [4] GMC Confidentiality: patients’ fitness to drive and reporting concerns to the DVLA (2017) · [5] Mental Capacity Act 2005 and Care Act 2014 · [6] NICE NG150 Supporting adult carers (2020)
knowledge.summary: A change in personality and conduct in a man of 58, with memory relatively spared and little insight, is behavioural-variant frontotemporal dementia until proved otherwise. It is often called a midlife crisis, stress or depression, which delays diagnosis. The GP’s job is a careful informant history, a screen for mimics (mood disorder, mania, alcohol, drugs, reversible physical causes), NG97 blood tests, and referral to a specialist dementia diagnostic service, with neurology or a young-onset service involved. A normal memory test does not exclude it. Address driving, money and safety now, raise lasting power of attorney while he may still have capacity, and support his wife as a carer.

points.t: Behavioural-variant FTD usually starts before 65. Consensus criteria [2] need three of six features for possible bvFTD: early disinhibition, early apathy or inertia, early loss of sympathy or empathy, perseverative or compulsive behaviour, hyperorality or dietary change, and an executive-led cognitive profile with relative sparing of memory and visuospatial skills. Insight is typically poor, so the informant history carries the diagnosis. Language variants present with progressive loss of speech or word meaning.

Depression, bipolar disorder or mania, late-onset psychosis, alcohol or drug misuse, medication effects, other dementias (Alzheimer’s is usually memory-led), and physical causes such as hypothyroidism, B12 deficiency, or a frontal space-occupying lesion. Ask about family history of dementia, motor neurone disease or psychiatric illness, and look for motor features: FTD can overlap with motor neurone disease.

NG97 [1]: take a history from the person and from someone who knows him well, supplemented where possible by a structured informant tool; examine; do blood tests to exclude reversible causes (FBC, ESR or CRP, calcium, HbA1c, renal and liver function, thyroid function, B12 and folate). Do not rule out dementia solely because the person has a normal score on a cognitive instrument: memory screens are often normal early in bvFTD.

Refer to a specialist dementia diagnostic service [1]; a young-onset service or cognitive neurology clinic is usually most appropriate at 58. Specialists arrange detailed neuropsychology and structural imaging, with perfusion or metabolic imaging if the diagnosis is uncertain. NG97: do not offer acetylcholinesterase inhibitors or memantine to people with frontotemporal dementia.

A person diagnosed with dementia must tell the DVLA [3]; the GMC [4] sets out when a doctor may inform the DVLA if a patient continues to drive when unsafe. Advise him not to drive while this is being assessed if there are concerns about judgement. Reckless spending exposes him and the household to financial harm: discuss practical protection and lasting power of attorney, which he can make only while he has capacity for that decision [5]. Consider safeguarding if he is being exploited.

His wife is a carer and is entitled to a carer’s assessment from the local authority under the Care Act 2014 [5]. NG150 [6] and NG97 [1] recommend identifying carers, offering information and support, and attending to their own health. Explaining that the behaviour is caused by an illness reduces blame and conflict.

dg.d: Consent from Brian for his wife to speak; lets her give the story uninterrupted.
Impact on the marriage and household finances; the carer’s own coping.
Examination including neurological and motor signs; NG97 bloods; recognises a normal memory screen does not exclude dementia.
bvFTD versus depression, mania, psychosis, alcohol or drugs, other dementias and structural or endocrine causes.
Headache, seizures, focal signs, rapid progression; motor neurone disease overlap; risk to self, others and finances.
Possible frontotemporal dementia named honestly as needing specialist assessment, not stress.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Referral to a specialist dementia diagnostic or young-onset service with neurology; tests explained; Brian’s agreement sought.
Driving stopped pending assessment and DVLA duty explained; financial protection and LPA while capacity lasts; carer’s assessment.
Same-day contact for rapid change or risk; review with results; referral chased; teach-back.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picks up poor insight, preserved memory and the “midlife crisis” label as cues rather than reassurance.
Wife’s idea (something is medically wrong), concern (what it is; money; the family), expectation (help and an explanation).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — Carol is frightened about money (the spending is draining their savings), about his driving, and that their marriage is over and she is scared of what it might be — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello, I’m Dr Patel. Thank you both for coming in. Brian, is it all right with you if your wife tells me what she has noticed, and then I’ll hear from you as well?
model.why: Addresses the patient first and gains consent for the collateral history

model.text: (Brian, shrugging) If she wants. I’m fine.

(Wife) I don’t recognise my husband any more. Over the last year or two he’s become rude and tactless. He says awful things in public. He’s spent thousands on nonsense, he doesn’t seem to care about anything or anyone, and he’s eating strangely. His memory’s actually fine. People say it’s a midlife crisis or stress, but this isn’t him.
Thank you. That sounds bewildering, and you’ve described it very clearly. You know him better than anyone, and I’m taking this seriously.
model.why: Validates the informant and signals it will not be dismissed

model.text: Can you give me an example of the sort of thing he says or does in public that is out of character?
(Wife) Comments about people that he’d never have made before. He doesn’t seem embarrassed at all afterwards.
And the change in caring: does he respond when you or others are upset? Has he lost interest in things he used to do?
(Wife) He just doesn’t react. It’s as if he’s switched off.
You mentioned eating strangely. What has changed? And does he do things repetitively or in a fixed routine?
model.why: Hyperorality and compulsive behaviour: consensus features

model.text: (Wife) It’s hard to describe. Just not how he used to eat. And yes, some things over and over.
Has his speech changed at all: finding words, understanding words, or speaking less? And any stiffness, weakness, falls or muscle twitching?
model.why: Language variant; parkinsonism and motor neurone disease overlap

model.text: (Wife) Not that I’ve noticed.
I need to check other things that can change someone’s behaviour. Brian, how has your mood been? Any times of feeling unusually high, full of energy, needing little sleep?
model.why: Depression and mania screen, asked of the patient

model.text: (Brian) No. I’m fine. Nothing’s wrong with me.
How much alcohol do you drink in a week, and do you take any other drugs or any medicines, including ones you buy?
model.why: Alcohol, drugs and medication as mimics

model.text: (Brian) Not much.
Any headaches, sickness, seizures or changes in vision? And is there anyone in the family who had dementia, motor neurone disease or a mental illness?
model.why: Structural lesion red flags; family history

model.text: (Wife) No headaches or anything like that. I don’t know of anything in the family.
A few important safety questions. Does Brian drive? And how is the money side: is the spending putting you under pressure, or has anyone taken advantage of him?
(Wife) The money really worries me. I haven’t known what to do about it.
Has anything happened that has put him or anyone else at risk, or made you feel unsafe at home?
model.why: Behavioural risk and the carer’s safety

model.text: (Wife) No, not like that. It’s just the way he is with people, and the money.
What have you been thinking this might be? And what worries you most?
(Wife) Everyone keeps saying stress. I think something is actually wrong with him. I’m frightened of what it is, and of what’s happening to us.

I don’t think this is a midlife crisis. A real change in personality over a year or two, at Brian’s age, with memory still good, can be caused by a condition affecting the front parts of the brain, called frontotemporal dementia. I can’t diagnose it today, and other things can look similar, but it needs a specialist assessment rather than being put down to stress.
model.why: Names the possibility honestly without over-committing

model.text: (Wife) Dementia? But his memory’s fine.

That’s why it is so often missed. This type usually affects behaviour, judgement and empathy first, and memory tests can be normal early on. Brian, I know you feel well in yourself. I’d still like to do some checks, because your wife has noticed real changes. Would you be willing?
model.why: Explains why normal memory fits; seeks the patient’s agreement despite poor insight

model.text: (Brian) If it keeps her happy.

Today I’ll examine you, and we’ll do blood tests to look for treatable causes: thyroid, vitamin levels, blood count, kidney, liver, calcium and sugar. I’ll refer you to a specialist memory and young-onset dementia service, with neurology input, for detailed thinking tests and a brain scan.
model.why: NG97 bloods; examination; specialist diagnostic referral

model.text: Two practical things now. Until the assessment is done, please don’t drive. If a diagnosis is made, there is a legal duty to tell the DVLA. And on money: it would be sensible to talk about protecting your joint finances, and about lasting power of attorney, which Brian can only set up while he is able to make that decision himself.
model.why: Driving and DVLA; financial protection; LPA while capacity lasts

model.text: And how are you coping? This is not his fault and not yours: if it is this illness, the behaviour comes from the brain changes. You are entitled to a carer’s assessment, and I can put you in touch with carer support.
model.why: Carer welfare, removes blame, signposts carer support

model.text: (Wife) Honestly, I’ve been struggling. It helps to hear someone say it isn’t just me.

If things change quickly, if he becomes unwell with headaches, confusion or weakness, or if anyone is at risk or you can’t cope, contact us the same day. Otherwise I’ll see you both once the blood results are back, and chase the referral. Can you tell me what we’ve agreed?
model.why: Safety-net for rapid change and risk; review; teach-back

model.text: (Wife) Blood tests, a referral to the specialist, no driving for now, sort out the money and the power of attorney, and support for me.
Exactly. I’ll record our conversation and I’ll book a double appointment for you both in two weeks.

social.t: Impulsive spending can cause serious debt. Practical steps include reviewing joint accounts, and the bank may offer support for vulnerable customers.
If Brian is working, his behaviour may put his job at risk. A diagnosis can open access to benefits and to employer adjustments or ill-health retirement.

legal.t: A person diagnosed with dementia must notify the DVLA. If he continues to drive when unsafe, GMC guidance (2017) sets out when a doctor may inform the DVLA.

Under the Mental Capacity Act 2005, capacity is decision-specific and assumed unless shown otherwise. Lasting power of attorney for property and finance, and for health and welfare, needs capacity at the time it is made.
If he is being financially exploited, a safeguarding concern can be raised with the local authority under the Care Act 2014.

professional.t: Seek Brian’s agreement to involve his wife; listening to an informant does not breach confidentiality, and sharing is guided by his consent and best interests.
Behavioural presentations are easily labelled psychiatric or relational. Keeping an organic cause in mind is part of safe practice.

community.t: Carer’s assessment from the local authority; national and local young-onset and frontotemporal dementia support groups; admiral nurses where available.

redFlags: Rapid progression, headache, seizures, vomiting or focal signs: structural lesion, urgent imaging
Weakness, wasting, fasciculation, swallowing or speech problems: FTD with motor neurone disease
Suicidal ideation, psychosis or mania: urgent mental health assessment
Financial exploitation or risk to others: safeguarding
psychosocial: Marriage under strain; wife as carer
ice: Idea (wife): something medically wrong, not a midlife crisis
Concern: what it is; money; the family

playbook.diagnosis: “This could be frontotemporal dementia, a condition affecting the front of the brain, which needs a specialist assessment.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “The front parts of the brain act like the brakes and the conscience: they stop us saying what we think and help us sense how others feel. If those parts are affected, a person can become tactless, impulsive and seem not to care, even though his memory is still good.”

management.reflectIce: “You felt this wasn’t really him, and I agree it needs looking into properly, not putting down to stress.”
management.psychosocial: Keep Brian involved and respected; support his wife as a carer; protect the household finances.
sharedPlan: Examination and NG97 blood tests for reversible causes
Referral to a specialist dementia diagnostic or young-onset service with neurology
No driving pending assessment; DVLA duty if diagnosed
Financial protection and LPA while capacity lasts
safetyNet: Rapid change, headache, seizures or weakness: same-day contact
Risk to Brian, others or finances, or carer not coping: contact the practice; review with results

pitfalls.intro: The history comes from his wife, and the trap is the “stress” label. Marks go to recognising a behaviour-led dementia with preserved memory, screening mimics, referring, and handling driving, money and the carer.

items.fail: Accepting stress, midlife crisis or depression without a collateral history.
items.why: This is the commonest reason FTD is diagnosed late.
items.fix: Take a structured informant history and screen mimics before labelling.

items.fail: Being reassured by good memory or a normal cognitive screen.
items.why: bvFTD spares memory early; NG97 warns against ruling out dementia on a normal score.
Impaired judgement puts him and others at risk; LPA needs capacity.
items.fix: Advise no driving pending assessment; explain the DVLA duty; raise LPA now.

items.fail: Talking about Brian as if he were not in the room.
items.why: He is the patient; ignoring him damages trust and consent.
items.fix: Ask his permission, address him directly, and seek his agreement to tests.

items.fail: Not asking how his wife is coping.
items.why: Carer strain is high and she is entitled to support.
items.fix: Ask directly, remove blame, offer a carer’s assessment.

items.fail: Starting a cognitive enhancer or antidepressant as the plan.
items.why: NG97: acetylcholinesterase inhibitors and memantine are not offered in FTD; the priority is diagnosis.
items.fix: Bloods, specialist referral, risk plan, review.

avoid.instead: “A real change in personality at his age needs a proper medical assessment.”

A few important safety questions. Does Brian drive? And how is the money side: is the spending putting you under pressure, or has anyone taken advantage of him?
(Wife) The money really worries me. I haven’t known what to do about it.
Has anything happened that has put him or anyone else at risk, or made you feel unsafe at home?
SCA_MODELS.why: Behavioural risk and the carer’s safety

SCA_MODELS.text: (Wife) No, not like that. It’s just the way he is with people, and the money.
What have you been thinking this might be? And what worries you most?
(Wife) Everyone keeps saying stress. I think something is actually wrong with him. I’m frightened of what it is, and of what’s happening to us.

I don’t think this is a midlife crisis. A real change in personality over a year or two, at Brian’s age, with memory still good, can be caused by a condition affecting the front parts of the brain, called frontotemporal dementia. I can’t diagnose it today, and other things can look similar, but it needs a specialist assessment rather than being put down to stress.
SCA_MODELS.why: Names the possibility honestly without over-committing

SCA_MODELS.text: (Wife) Dementia? But his memory’s fine.

That’s why it is so often missed. This type usually affects behaviour, judgement and empathy first, and memory tests can be normal early on. Brian, I know you feel well in yourself. I’d still like to do some checks, because your wife has noticed real changes. Would you be willing?
SCA_MODELS.why: Explains why normal memory fits; seeks the patient’s agreement despite poor insight

SCA_MODELS.text: (Brian) If it keeps her happy.

Today I’ll examine you, and we’ll do blood tests to look for treatable causes: thyroid, vitamin levels, blood count, kidney, liver, calcium and sugar. I’ll refer you to a specialist memory and young-onset dementia service, with neurology input, for detailed thinking tests and a brain scan.
SCA_MODELS.why: NG97 bloods; examination; specialist diagnostic referral

SCA_MODELS.text: Two practical things now. Until the assessment is done, please don’t drive. If a diagnosis is made, there is a legal duty to tell the DVLA. And on money: it would be sensible to talk about protecting your joint finances, and about lasting power of attorney, which Brian can only set up while he is able to make that decision himself.
SCA_MODELS.why: Driving and DVLA; financial protection; LPA while capacity lasts

SCA_MODELS.text: And how are you coping? This is not his fault and not yours: if it is this illness, the behaviour comes from the brain changes. You are entitled to a carer’s assessment, and I can put you in touch with carer support.
SCA_MODELS.why: Carer welfare, removes blame, signposts carer support

SCA_MODELS.text: (Wife) Honestly, I’ve been struggling. It helps to hear someone say it isn’t just me.

If things change quickly, if he becomes unwell with headaches, confusion or weakness, or if anyone is at risk or you can’t cope, contact us the same day. Otherwise I’ll see you both once the blood results are back, and chase the referral. Can you tell me what we’ve agreed?
SCA_MODELS.why: Safety-net for rapid change and risk; review; teach-back

SCA_MODELS.text: (Wife) Blood tests, a referral to the specialist, no driving for now, sort out the money and the power of attorney, and support for me.
Exactly. I’ll record our conversation and I’ll book a double appointment for you both in two weeks.

SCA_STEM.recent: Wife reports one to two years of progressive change in personality and behaviour: rude, tactless remarks in public, thousands spent on “nonsense”, seems not to care about anything or anyone, eating strangely. Memory said to be fine. Others have put it down to a midlife crisis or stress.
SCA_STEM.reason: Attends with his wife: “I don’t recognise my husband any more.” Brian does not think anything is wrong.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: [1] NICE NG97 Dementia: assessment, management and support for people living with dementia and their carers (2018) · [2] International consensus criteria for behavioural-variant frontotemporal dementia, Rascovsky et al., Brain 2011 (international) · [3] DVLA Assessing fitness to drive: dementia · [4] GMC Confidentiality: patients’ fitness to drive and reporting concerns to the DVLA (2017) · [5] Mental Capacity Act 2005 and Care Act 2014 · [6] NICE NG150 Supporting adult carers (2020)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: A change in personality and conduct in a man of 58, with memory relatively spared and little insight, is behavioural-variant frontotemporal dementia until proved otherwise. It is often called a midlife crisis, stress or depression, which delays diagnosis. The GP’s job is a careful informant history, a screen for mimics (mood disorder, mania, alcohol, drugs, reversible physical causes), NG97 blood tests, and referral to a specialist dementia diagnostic service, with neurology or a young-onset service involved. A normal memory test does not exclude it. Address driving, money and safety now, raise lasting power of attorney while he may still have capacity, and support his wife as a carer.

points.t: Behavioural-variant FTD usually starts before 65. Consensus criteria [2] need three of six features for possible bvFTD: early disinhibition, early apathy or inertia, early loss of sympathy or empathy, perseverative or compulsive behaviour, hyperorality or dietary change, and an executive-led cognitive profile with relative sparing of memory and visuospatial skills. Insight is typically poor, so the informant history carries the diagnosis. Language variants present with progressive loss of speech or word meaning.

Depression, bipolar disorder or mania, late-onset psychosis, alcohol or drug misuse, medication effects, other dementias (Alzheimer’s is usually memory-led), and physical causes such as hypothyroidism, B12 deficiency, or a frontal space-occupying lesion. Ask about family history of dementia, motor neurone disease or psychiatric illness, and look for motor features: FTD can overlap with motor neurone disease.

NG97 [1]: take a history from the person and from someone who knows him well, supplemented where possible by a structured informant tool; examine; do blood tests to exclude reversible causes (FBC, ESR or CRP, calcium, HbA1c, renal and liver function, thyroid function, B12 and folate). Do not rule out dementia solely because the person has a normal score on a cognitive instrument: memory screens are often normal early in bvFTD.

Refer to a specialist dementia diagnostic service [1]; a young-onset service or cognitive neurology clinic is usually most appropriate at 58. Specialists arrange detailed neuropsychology and structural imaging, with perfusion or metabolic imaging if the diagnosis is uncertain. NG97: do not offer acetylcholinesterase inhibitors or memantine to people with frontotemporal dementia.

A person diagnosed with dementia must tell the DVLA [3]; the GMC [4] sets out when a doctor may inform the DVLA if a patient continues to drive when unsafe. Advise him not to drive while this is being assessed if there are concerns about judgement. Reckless spending exposes him and the household to financial harm: discuss practical protection and lasting power of attorney, which he can make only while he has capacity for that decision [5]. Consider safeguarding if he is being exploited.

His wife is a carer and is entitled to a carer’s assessment from the local authority under the Care Act 2014 [5]. NG150 [6] and NG97 [1] recommend identifying carers, offering information and support, and attending to their own health. Explaining that the behaviour is caused by an illness reduces blame and conflict.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Consent from Brian for his wife to speak; lets her give the story uninterrupted.
Impact on the marriage and household finances; the carer’s own coping.
Picks up poor insight, preserved memory and the “midlife crisis” label as cues rather than reassurance.
Wife’s idea (something is medically wrong), concern (what it is; money; the family), expectation (help and an explanation).
Examination including neurological and motor signs; NG97 bloods; recognises a normal memory screen does not exclude dementia.
bvFTD versus depression, mania, psychosis, alcohol or drugs, other dementias and structural or endocrine causes.
Headache, seizures, focal signs, rapid progression; motor neurone disease overlap; risk to self, others and finances.
Possible frontotemporal dementia named honestly as needing specialist assessment, not stress.
Referral to a specialist dementia diagnostic or young-onset service with neurology; tests explained; Brian’s agreement sought.
Driving stopped pending assessment and DVLA duty explained; financial protection and LPA while capacity lasts; carer’s assessment.
Same-day contact for rapid change or risk; review with results; referral chased; teach-back.

social.t: Impulsive spending can cause serious debt. Practical steps include reviewing joint accounts, and the bank may offer support for vulnerable customers.
If Brian is working, his behaviour may put his job at risk. A diagnosis can open access to benefits and to employer adjustments or ill-health retirement.

legal.t: A person diagnosed with dementia must notify the DVLA. If he continues to drive when unsafe, GMC guidance (2017) sets out when a doctor may inform the DVLA.

Under the Mental Capacity Act 2005, capacity is decision-specific and assumed unless shown otherwise. Lasting power of attorney for property and finance, and for health and welfare, needs capacity at the time it is made.
If he is being financially exploited, a safeguarding concern can be raised with the local authority under the Care Act 2014.

professional.t: Seek Brian’s agreement to involve his wife; listening to an informant does not breach confidentiality, and sharing is guided by his consent and best interests.
Behavioural presentations are easily labelled psychiatric or relational. Keeping an organic cause in mind is part of safe practice.

community.t: Carer’s assessment from the local authority; national and local young-onset and frontotemporal dementia support groups; admiral nurses where available.

redFlags: Rapid progression, headache, seizures, vomiting or focal signs: structural lesion, urgent imaging
Weakness, wasting, fasciculation, swallowing or speech problems: FTD with motor neurone disease
Suicidal ideation, psychosis or mania: urgent mental health assessment
Financial exploitation or risk to others: safeguarding
psychosocial: Marriage under strain; wife as carer
ice: Idea (wife): something medically wrong, not a midlife crisis
Concern: what it is; money; the family

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “This could be frontotemporal dementia, a condition affecting the front of the brain, which needs a specialist assessment.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “The front parts of the brain act like the brakes and the conscience: they stop us saying what we think and help us sense how others feel. If those parts are affected, a person can become tactless, impulsive and seem not to care, even though his memory is still good.”

management.reflectIce: “You felt this wasn’t really him, and I agree it needs looking into properly, not putting down to stress.”
management.psychosocial: Keep Brian involved and respected; support his wife as a carer; protect the household finances.

safetyNet: Rapid change, headache, seizures or weakness: same-day contact
Risk to Brian, others or finances, or carer not coping: contact the practice; review with results

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: The history comes from his wife, and the trap is the “stress” label. Marks go to recognising a behaviour-led dementia with preserved memory, screening mimics, referring, and handling driving, money and the carer.

items.fail: Accepting stress, midlife crisis or depression without a collateral history.
items.why: This is the commonest reason FTD is diagnosed late.
items.fix: Take a structured informant history and screen mimics before labelling.

items.fail: Being reassured by good memory or a normal cognitive screen.
items.why: bvFTD spares memory early; NG97 warns against ruling out dementia on a normal score.
Impaired judgement puts him and others at risk; LPA needs capacity.
items.fix: Advise no driving pending assessment; explain the DVLA duty; raise LPA now.

items.fail: Talking about Brian as if he were not in the room.
items.why: He is the patient; ignoring him damages trust and consent.
items.fix: Ask his permission, address him directly, and seek his agreement to tests.

items.fail: Not asking how his wife is coping.
items.why: Carer strain is high and she is entitled to support.
items.fix: Ask directly, remove blame, offer a carer’s assessment.

items.fail: Starting a cognitive enhancer or antidepressant as the plan.
items.why: NG97: acetylcholinesterase inhibitors and memantine are not offered in FTD; the priority is diagnosis.
items.fix: Bloods, specialist referral, risk plan, review.
